results.title: How can I contact support?
results.content:
Navigate to the "Network" tab.

Enable the "Preserve log" checkbox.

Click the "crossed circle" button to clear any existing logs from the Network tab.

(Important) Reproduce the issue while the network requests are recorded (specifically, perform the actions that lead to an error or other unexpected behavior that you are concerned about).

Click the download icon ("Export HAR (sanitized)..." button) to save the file to your computer. [...] ## Recording a HAR file for Troubleshooting UI Issues

In order to help with various issues with Interface of ChatGPT, Platform and other products, ChatGPT Conversations or other non-API-related scenarios, Support team may ask you to record a HAR file in your browser for replicating the issue.  
  
A HAR file, or HTTP Archive file, is a JSON-formatted archive that logs a web browser's interactions with a website. It captures details like requests, responses, headers, and timings, making it useful for troubleshooting and performance analysis  
  
  
Recording a HAR File is easy and does not require technical skills.  
  
See steps below:

Open Developer Tools by right-clicking the webpage and selecting "Inspect", or by pressing Ctrl+Shift+I (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Opt+I (Mac). [...] You can use this video guide (not affiliated with OpenAI) as a reference point.  
  
Please be informed that HAR files may include personal or other sensitive data. You can use a tool like Cloudflare's HAR sanitizer to remove any personal information before sharing. Some browsers, like Google Chrome, automatically sanitize the HAR file when saving.  
  
Note: The ChatGPT desktop app does not currently provide developer tools for HAR capture. If your HAR file exceeds the 25 MB attachment limit, upload it to a secure cloud storage location (e.g., Google Drive or Dropbox) and share a view-only link in your support ticket.

results.title: Stop Complaining About Broken Systems and Ask This Instead
results.content:
On the flip side, if you're a customer, citizen, or resident and the government is doing something a certain way, rather than complain about it, ask questions.

Rather than rage posting, ask questions.

If you're a local and you don't understand something happening in immigrant communities, rather than complain, maybe you should go to those communities and ask questions. Go to those micro community leaders and ask questions.

That's where beautiful energy exists. That's where resourceful problem-solving lives.

### The Question Before All Questions

Research from Harvard shows that strategic questioning "spurs learning and the exchange of ideas, fuels innovation and performance improvement." Yet few executives think of questioning as a skill that can be honed. [...] ### Why Complaining Reinforces the Problem

Research on complaining psychology shows that much of it "falls into the category of ego reinforcement" rather than genuine problem-solving.

When you complain, you're stating a conclusion without examining the mechanism. You're saying "this is broken" without asking "how does this actually work?"

I've worked across entertainment, sports, government ministries, and corporate boardrooms. From Portugal to the New Zealand, Kentucky to the Middle East. And here's what I've learned: every system runs on people making decisions based on incomplete information and inherited processes.

Questions expose those gaps. Complaints reinforce them.

### Listening for What They're Not Saying [...] When people feel like you're trying to trap them or prove them wrong, they shut down immediately. But when they feel like you actually want to understand, most people open up.

Instead of "Why is this so inefficient?" (which is basically a complaint disguised as a question), I'll ask "Help me understand what happens when..." or "Walk me through how this works from your perspective."

That language signals I'm trying to see it through their eyes, not judge it from mine.

I also ask questions that assume good intent. Instead of "Why hasn't anyone fixed this?" I'll ask "What would need to change for this to work differently?"

That question assumes they've probably thought about it, maybe even tried to change it, and there are real barriers. And often, that's when the real reason comes out.
